newsitem.title: GREECE: GNN BOND GUIDE - MONTE CARLO SIMULATION METHOD.
newsitem.headline: GNN BOND GUIDE - MONTE CARLO SIMULATION METHOD.

text.p: We proceed today with a brief
description of the Monte Carlo method which is a simulation
study designed to shed light on the small-sample properties of
competing outcomes for a given problem in business management
and narrower fields such as finance.
The Monte Carlo method is the most commonly used valuation
method of interest rate instruments such as bonds with embedded
options, FRNs, interest rate caps and floors.
The general steps of the simulation in statistics are:
1) Model the data generating process
2) Generate several sets of artificial data
3) Employ the data and the estimator to create several
estimates
4) Use the estimates to gauge the sampling distribution
properties of that estimator.
The same structure characterizes the Monte Carlo valuation
method of interest rate financial instruments.
We outline the steps for the valuation of interest rate
instruments embodied in commercial packages. What follows is
what we know from Wall Street.
It should be noted that the Monte Carlo simulation has been
limited to the theoretical value of the bond in question, that
is the average price of the process, ignoring information about
the probability distribution.
VALUATION STEPS:
1) Input the current term structure of spot interest rates
and assume some degree of volatility that will constrain the
dispersion of future interest rates in the simulation and ensure
that the average simulated price of the instrument is the
current market price.
The market calibration of the model is common practice and
usually takes the form of inserting a drift term in the model so
that market price equals the Monte Carlo value for the security.
2) Make sure that the model is arbitrage free, that is no
arbitrage is possible in future dates among interest rates.
3) Calculate the present value of the cash flows for each
interest rate path by discounting them with the simulated spot
rates calculated from the simulated future rates.
To save computational time, the number of interest rate
paths is limited by a price convergence figure, typically a
tick. In other words, the number of rate paths is determined
when price estimates from the model do not chnage by more than a
tick.
It should also be pointed out that the model is constructed
in such a way as to rule out interest rate outliers (negative
nominal interest rates etc.). This is achieved by the so called
interest rate mean reversion. In other words, the interest rate
is forced back to an average value after hitting the outer
interest rate frontier set in advance.
4) Average all present values on all interest rate paths to
come up with the theoretical value of the security.
Monte Carlo simulation is also used to get measures of
option-adjusted duration and convexity for nonparallel shifts in
the yield curve.
--Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
